Eye contact is not just "eye contact," and some people don't realize this. Often, you can tell when someone is making eye contact just to make eye contact, and they often have these unnatural, wide-open eyes that are clearly strained.

Or, while you are "trying" to make eye contact, they make eye contact with you, and then you shift your mannerism somehow, or your eyes get larger, or whatever, even in the most subtle way, to their eyes, makes it come off as creepy. Eye contact is important, but it needs to be natural, and this is a hard challenge for a lot of people.

Also, natural eye contact is not 100% staring into their eyes; no one does that naturally. It's looking at their eyes but letting your gaze wander a little to their lips, or looking away while you think of a response. This is more natural. I have an acquaintance who doesn't get this, and you can tell he is trying to have eye contact, but instead, he just stares at you because of the never-ending "stare." And that is the key word: good eye contact is NOT staring; it is, as I said, looking into their eyes but not penetrating their gaze, not being afraid to look at their lips or something else when you think. Looking at their eyes can be great, especially with someone of the opposite sex, but if you are going to intensely focus on their eyes, it better be with someone with whom you know there is a good vibe.

As for hovering, I don't know. This usually just means people don't want you to be "in" on their conversation, but you hang around anyway, missing the social cues. There could be many reasons why they may not want this, but typically if someone is already engaged in a conversation, and you show up, if they don't immediately bring you into it after the initial "hey, how's it going?" then just move on. You might say, "What's new?" and if it doesn't go beyond a "not much..." then just say, "Oh, just wanted to say hey, don't want to interrupt your conversation. I'll see you later!" Then move on. Hoverers don't get the social cues and still hang around.

I am not saying this is your case, but the situation is situational. You can be the most popular person around, but that doesn't mean that a certain conversation is meant for you to be a part of. Not everyone wants you to be a part of every conversation, so don't take it as a personal slight against you if they don't want you to be. The popular person gets this, understands this, and moves on quickly. No lingering, no awkward pauses, just, "See you later!" But if you are asking yourself why you may not be the person that gets brought into the conversations, there are many reasons this could be. It's true what others have said; being attractive helps, but that's not really it. All that does is help you jump through a few hoops. If you are still "weird," then people will catch on soon enough, no matter how good-looking you are. A lot of it has to do with the perception that people don't think you have something to bring to the conversation. People enjoy others who have an interesting life, have interesting stories to share, or things they can relate to. If you are NEVER the person to talk about cool things you did that weekend, or places you went, or relevant things to others, and being able to do so in an interesting way, it is harder for them to even care about sharing anything with you.

My go-to success in social situations is to have your own interesting things about yourself but to spend 90% of the time talking about things they care about. See them talking about something? Ask them a cool question about it, show interest in their topic. Focus on them, and they will appreciate you. Again, this needs to be natural, and you need to show sincere interest; questions can't be technical and just for gaining information, but more along the lines of, "Oh wow, that sounds like it was so fun, did you manage to do this too when you did it?!" Just as a brief example...

Ultimately, though, the key is to be able to predict how other people might react to what you say and do, and being able to do that on the fly, without thinking about it much. Meaning, if I act a certain way and I do a certain thing, what are these people going to think? Being able to "know" how people will react rather than just guess or try to think how they will is the highest quality to have that will help you succeed in social situations more. It allows flexibility, the ability to discern people's different personalities and how to react to each one appropriately. It will allow you to catch the social cues more quickly because you can discern what others might be thinking. Some of this comes from experience, but much of it just comes from self-awareness.

This is all easier said than done, and it is hard to say it is something that can be "practiced." Why? Because much of it you can't really... However, the important thing is this: If YOU like yourself, and you know what you want in your life, and are going for it, then you will have the self-confidence to be that kind of person. Just know what you want out of life and go for it. If you don't, that's step one. You can't go any further if you are just going to doubt yourself. The reality is that it all falls back on you, and you CAN and absolutely will become someone who is likable and successful, in whatever way that definition of success matters to you, but you first have to believe in yourself that, one, you are not some creep, because you're not, and then go from there.

You could have a refresh rate of 288hz and it wouldn't make your game more smooth if your graphics processing unit couldn't output that. The nice thing is that super high refresh rates allow you to achieve things like 3D gaming and/or reduce motion blur. These are things that even being able to run a game at 60fps is not enough.

So, where adaptive sync technologies shine is at lower FPS. Screen tearing happens at low FPS. It technically happens at high FPS too, but because high FPS is so high you don't really notice it. At low FPS it is VERY obvious... so that is where adaptive sync really shines. It will not really be all that useful if you even have a moderately powerful system on older games and can pull 60+ FPS. However, even the latest high-end video cards can't push the newest games at high resolutions at 60 FPS (for now lol), so for serious enthusiasts you really need this kind of adaptive sync monitor to get the smoothest experience as possible.

Anyway, it's one of those things you don't realize you needed until you have it. I used to be stubborn, never really thought screen tearing was all that bad, and then I was at a friend's house and saw how smooth his games were... it was weird not seeing the jitter, even on his weaker gaming system, but superior monitor. I felt a strong revelation come over me and knew that I needed something like that. So, I got myself an adaptive sync monitor and never looked back. I only have 1, in a 3 monitor setup (not for triple monitor gaming but for work purposes, I only game on the adaptive sync monitor), but oh man is it just amazing...

Even better, adaptive sync as of the last major graphics driver update a couple weeks back, now works in windowed mode (used to be fullscreen gaming only). As a big multi-tasker this was critical to me. I can't speak for the other adaptive sync technology but the tech seems similar.

In a country in southern Africa, the wildlife reserves are referred to as "game parks." When discussing wildlife, the common term used is "game." While it may sound like a hunting term to someone from the United States, it is simply the standard terminology in the English spoken in that region. Thus, "game reserve" or "game park" are commonly used phrases. These are enclosed areas with wildlife that differ from a zoo, consisting of vast expanses of land fenced off for visitors to drive through and observe animals in their natural environment. The largest park, a well-known national park, is the biggest game reserve in the world, spanning thousands of square miles of protected land.

Ideally, these areas are meant to be free from poachers, but there are instances where they may cut the fences to gain access, particularly in the largest park.

There are specific game parks designed for hunters, but once again, "game" is a universal term used to describe wildlife.

You can easily play and stream locally a 1080P signal on something as weak as a small single-board computer. This is not going to be an issue for practically any device you run. Integrated graphics are more than enough to handle a 1080P signal flawlessly.

A network-attached storage system also requires very little processing power. Just remember a NAS just means Network Attached Storage. You can just throw in a bunch of hard drives (if you want, RAID them for one giant drive, but this has risks if you don't have an auto-backup system, as if one drive goes out, you lose the data on ALL drives), and then connect the system to your home network, allowing the folders to be "shared" between devices. Boom, it's that simple, all of a sudden you have a NAS.

Now, this is where the operating system comes into play, and in my opinion, it seems like your only two real options here are either some Linux distribution or a version of Windows. Typically, if it was ONLY a NAS, you could install some really lightweight server program to manage the data, but since you want to have a gaming platform on it AND you want it to be your media center AND you want it to be your NAS, you need something that can do all of the above. Windows is kind of overkill, but it is also incredibly easy to use and get most of the programs up and running without issues or much tinkering to get all your drivers working right. If you are comfortable with the command line, it's nice to go with Linux as you can just SSH into your system, but since you said you are looking to remote desktop to it, a certain version of Windows has remote desktop built in. Either way, the latest version coming out for free soon if you have a previous license, so ultimately it does have such a feature. Eh, programmer here. A lot of people outside of the industry don't realize how overwhelming and massive a coding project can be, even for small programs. They can be extremely mentally exhausting, to the point that when you have a good idea, as an experienced coder you also then think to yourself, "But wow, it is going to be a hell of a lot of work, is it worth it!?"

For example, I built a "small" side addon for a popular online game, just as a side hobby "fun" project, and this fun little side project blossomed into about 10k lines of code, with people requesting features, UI tweaks, and so on. This was a "small" side project. I think a lot of people don't understand the massive amount of work involved with writing code.

It was "sort of" fun for a little while, when you were just feature building and infrastructure building. But, retroactively changing things for the better while not breaking old database management methods and so on will be a soul-sucking, caffeine-binging epidemic that happens on *EVERY* project, without fail. It is the nature of the industry. You trust yourself that you will find a solution, and you always do. In fact, I have never, to this day, not built a solution to what I wanted to do. But damn if it is not an occasional rough experience.

Every "fun hobby side project" will have these moments, and before you start any of them, as an experienced coder, you are completely self-aware of the challenges that lie before you. When you are younger, you think, "Worth it!" Things change when you get older and priorities shift and time availability changes.

This will act as a barrier at some point in your career. When you are young, no family, no kids, sleep 4hrs a night, it's not a big deal. When you gain other hobbies (which is much easier to gain now that you have more money as a coder), all of a sudden you don't necessarily have the "itch" to sit behind a computer and code for 12hrs a day.
